common_name: Success Saskatoon Serviceberry (Historic Early-Ripening Western Serviceberry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Success is self-fertile but sets heavier crops with a second saskatoon cultivar nearby, and its early bloom means a sheltered site helps it dodge late prairie frosts.

directions: Success is one of the oldest named saskatoon cultivars still grown today, selected generations ago from wild Amelanchier alnifolia stands on the Canadian prairies for its heavy, reliable cropping rather than for exceptional berry size. Clusters of white flowers open in early spring on multi-stemmed, upright shrubs, followed by sweet, mild, purple-blue berries that ripen several days to two weeks earlier than newer cultivars like Northline or Parkhill, making it useful for spreading out a harvest window. Fruit is smaller than modern selections but produced in heavy quantity, and the plant suckers readily to form a productive thicket over time. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; it is exceptionally cold-hardy and requires little care beyond periodic removal of old canes to keep new, more fruitful wood coming.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program — Saskatoon Cultivar Trials
Government of Saskatchewan — Saskatoon Berry Production

common_name: Cardinal Royal Mountain Ash (Michred European Mountain Ash)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Cardinal Royal was patented (as Michred) for its uniform, symmetrical habit and is typically grown as a single-leader specimen or street tree.

directions: Cardinal Royal, patented under the name Michred by Michigan State University, is a European mountain ash selection prized for a tighter, more symmetrical oval crown than seedling-grown Sorbus aucuparia and for berries that ripen a deeper, brighter red rather than the species' typical orange. Flat clusters of white flowers open in late spring, and the compound, fern-like leaves turn shades of orange and red in fall alongside the heavy berry clusters that persist into winter and draw waxwings and other fruit-eating birds. The tart berries can be cooked into jelly once softened by frost. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; like other mountain ash, it performs best in cool-summer climates and struggles with borers and fire blight in hot, humid regions, so it is best suited to the northern tier of its hardiness range.
sources: Michigan State University plant patent records

common_name: Spring Glow Cornelian Cherry (Low-Chill Southern Cornelian Cherry Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Spring Glow has a notably low chill requirement, making it one of the few Cornus mas selections reliable in warm-winter southern gardens, and benefits from a second cornelian cherry nearby for best fruit set.

directions: Spring Glow is an introduction from the J.C. Raulston Arboretum selected for its notably low chilling requirement, extending the range of cornelian cherry into warmer parts of the South where most European-bred Cornus mas cultivars bloom poorly or fail to set fruit. Hundreds of small, bright yellow flowers smother the bare branches in late winter to early spring, weeks ahead of forsythia, followed by glossy, leathery dark-green summer foliage and oblong, cherry-red fruit that ripens in midsummer. The tart, plum-like fruit drops as it softens and is best gathered daily from a tarp or the ground for use in syrups, jams, and preserves. This small multi-stemmed tree tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soils, and is largely free of the pests and diseases that trouble other stone fruits, making it a low-maintenance choice for southern edible landscapes.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cornus mas

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; like the species, Ragin Cajun resents root disturbance once settled, so choose its permanent spot at planting time.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to light shade. Ragin Cajun is a Juniper Level Botanic Garden/Plant Delights Nursery selection made in 2000 near St. Francisville, Louisiana, prized for producing roughly a third more flowering stems than typical seed-grown Indian pink, making for a denser, showier clump in a compact 20-inch frame. Its tubular flowers lean more orange-red than the blood-red of most forms in the trade, with the same bright yellow, star-shaped throat that makes this plant one of the finest native hummingbird magnets for a shaded garden. Blooms open in mid-to-late spring and continue into midsummer; pair with ferns, wild ginger, or woodland phlox and leave it undisturbed once established.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; surface-sow without covering, as seeds need light to germinate. Isolate from red-flowered cardinal flower if seed-saving, since this white form breeds true only when self-pollinated.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun — rain gardens, stream banks, and pond margins suit this plant perfectly. White Cardinal is a stable, naturally occurring white-flowered form of the native cardinal flower, its pristine white tubular spikes rising above a basal rosette of chartreuse foliage and appearing to hover along the tall stems in dappled light. Flowers open from midsummer into fall and remain just as attractive to hummingbirds and butterflies as the typical scarlet form, offering an unexpected color break for a white or moon garden planted near water. Like the species, individual plants are short-lived, so allow some self-sowing or divide offsets to maintain the colony.
